title: Docker containers, cgroups, and CI/CD pipelines
description: Docker layer caching, multi-stage builds, Linux cgroups v2 resource limits, and CI/CD security.

questions.text: Why should 'COPY package*.json ./' and 'npm install' precede 'COPY . .' in a production Node.js Dockerfile?

options.text: To prevent npm from running as root
To leverage Docker layer caching: dependencies are only re-installed when package files change, speeding up CI builds when only application source code is modified
Because npm install requires an empty working directory

questions.explanation: Docker caches intermediate layers. If `COPY . .` is executed first, any tiny change to a source file or README invalidates all subsequent layers, forcing an expensive and slow `npm install` on every single commit.

questions.text: What is the primary security advantage of Docker Multi-Stage builds for compiled or bundled languages (Go, Rust, Java, TypeScript)?

options.text: It encrypts container disk volumes at rest

It leaves compilers, build tools, package managers, and source code in the build stage, producing a minimal final runtime container (e.g. distroless or alpine) with a drastically reduced CVE attack surface
It enables GPU acceleration for backend microservices
It runs containers without Linux kernel namespaces

questions.explanation: Compilers (GCC, Rustc, Go SDK) and package managers contain thousands of utilities that attackers can abuse if a container is compromised. Multi-stage builds copy only the compiled static binary into a clean runtime base, reducing image size from 1GB to 25MB and eliminating vulnerable binaries.

questions.text: When a container in Kubernetes exceeds its configured 'resources.limits.memory', what action does the Linux kernel take?

options.text: It throttles container CPU cycles until memory usage subsides
The Linux cgroups Out-Of-Memory (OOM) Killer immediately sends SIGKILL (exit code 137) to terminate the primary container process
It automatically expands the node's physical RAM swap file
It writes active memory pages to disk without stopping execution

questions.explanation: Unlike CPU limits (which cause throttling via CFS bandwidth quotas), memory cannot be compressed. When a container exceeds its cgroup hard memory limit, the kernel OOM Killer immediately terminates it with `SIGKILL` (reported as `OOMKilled` / Exit Code 137 in Kubernetes).

questions.text: Why is running a containerized production backend as the default 'root' (UID 0) user considered a dangerous security antipattern?

options.text: Because root processes cannot open ports below 1024
Because container UID 0 is mapped directly to the host's UID 0; a container breakout vulnerability grants the attacker full root control over the underlying host node
Because Linux terminates root containers after 24 hours
Because root containers cannot read environment variables

questions.explanation: Unless user namespaces (userns-remap) are configured, root inside a container is root on the host machine. If an attacker exploits a remote code execution or container breakout flaw, they immediately gain kernel-level host access.

questions.text: In Linux cgroups v2, CPU limits do not kill the container; instead, the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) throttles CPU time slices within the enforcement period.
questions.explanation: True. If a container exceeds its CPU limit (e.g. 500m / 0.5 CPU cores), the CFS scheduler simply halts thread execution until the next 100ms quota period begins, causing latency spikes without process termination.
